title: API Design: REST, gRPC & GraphQL
tagline: How services talk to each other and to clients — and how to design endpoints an interviewer respects.
summary: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL, idempotency, pagination, versioning.

items.detail: Resources (nouns) addressed by URLs, manipulated with HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) over JSON. Simple, cacheable (GETs), universally supported, human-readable. The default for public/client-facing APIs.
Binary RPC over HTTP/2 using Protocol Buffers. Compact, fast, strongly-typed contracts, supports streaming. The default for *internal* service-to-service communication where performance matters.

A query language where the *client* specifies exactly the fields it wants in one request. Eliminates over-/under-fetching and request waterfalls; great for varied clients (mobile vs web). Cost: harder caching, complex server, risk of expensive queries.

blocks.text: Common real-world split: REST or GraphQL at the edge for clients, gRPC between internal services. State this and you've shown you know where each shines rather than treating them as competitors.

items.detail: `POST /users`, `GET /users/123`, `GET /users/123/orders` — not `/createUser`. Let HTTP verbs convey the action.

items.term: Use the right verbs & status codes
items.detail: GET (read), POST (create → 201), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE. Return 200/201/204, 400/401/403/404/409/429, 500/503 meaningfully.
GET/PUT/DELETE should be idempotent (safe to retry). For POST (e.g., 'create payment'), accept an **Idempotency-Key** header so a client retry doesn't create duplicates.

Never return unbounded lists. Use **cursor-based** pagination (a token pointing past the last item) for large/changing datasets — it's stable and scalable; offset/limit drifts and gets slow deep in the list.
Version the API (`/v1/...` or a header) so you can evolve without breaking existing clients.
Support query params for filtering/sorting and returning only needed fields, to reduce payloads.

blocks.title: Cursor vs offset pagination
blocks.text: Offset/limit (`?page=500`) forces the DB to scan and skip rows (slow at depth) and items shift if data is inserted/deleted mid-scroll. Cursor pagination (`?after=<id/timestamp>`) seeks directly and is stable under writes — the right answer for feeds, timelines, and large lists.

paragraphs: In a system design interview, sketching the API is a key step — it forces clarity on what the system does. For each core feature, write the endpoint, its inputs, and outputs. Example for a URL shortener: `POST /urls {longUrl} → {shortUrl}` and `GET /{shortCode} → 302 redirect`. This 'API contract' anchors the rest of the design (data model, services) and shows structured thinking.

Treat the API as a stable contract: backward-compatible changes (adding optional fields) are safe; breaking changes (removing/renaming fields) need a new version. Good APIs are predictable, consistent in naming, and document their errors.

cheatsheet: REST (JSON/HTTP) for public/CRUD APIs; gRPC (Protobuf/HTTP2) for fast internal service calls; GraphQL to avoid over/under-fetch for varied clients.
REST design: resource nouns, correct verbs/status codes, version the API.
Make GET/PUT/DELETE idempotent; for POST use an Idempotency-Key so retries don't duplicate.
Use cursor-based pagination for large/changing lists (stable + fast); avoid deep offset/limit.
Sketch the API contract early in interviews — it anchors data model and services and signals structure.

questions.prompt: A 'Pay' button sometimes double-charges users on flaky networks because the client retries the POST. How do you fix this at the API level?
questions.hint: POST isn't idempotent by default. Give the client a way to mark 'this is the same request'.
answer: The retried POST creates a second charge because POST is not idempotent. Fix it with an **idempotency key**: the client generates a unique key per payment attempt and sends it as a header (`Idempotency-Key`). The server records the key with the result of the first successful processing; if a request arrives with a key it has already seen, it returns the original result instead of charging again.

Store the key→result mapping durably (with a TTL) and write the charge + key atomically so a crash mid-processing can't create a duplicate. This turns an unsafe retry into a safe no-op and is the standard pattern payment APIs (Stripe, etc.) use.
keyPoints: Server dedupes: return stored result for seen keys
Atomic charge + key write; key store with TTL
followUps: How does this relate to at-least-once message delivery and idempotent consumers?

questions.prompt: Your mobile app makes 6 sequential REST calls to render one screen, causing slow loads. Would GraphQL or gRPC help, and what's the catch?
questions.hint: The problem is multiple round trips / over-fetching.
answer: **GraphQL** directly targets this: the client asks for exactly the data the screen needs across multiple resources in a *single* request, eliminating the 6-round-trip waterfall and over-fetching. That's its core strength for rich, data-aggregating clients.

The catch: GraphQL makes HTTP caching harder (one endpoint, POST queries), and you must guard against expensive/abusive queries (query depth/cost limits, persisted queries). A simpler alternative is a REST **Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)** that aggregates the 6 calls server-side into one response — keeps REST's caching simplicity while cutting client round trips. gRPC helps internal call latency but wouldn't by itself collapse the 6 client requests.
keyPoints: GraphQL collapses many resource fetches into one request, no over-fetch
Catch: harder caching + must limit query cost
gRPC speeds internal calls, not the client round-trip count
followUps: When would a BFF be preferable to exposing GraphQL directly?
